# Modules and repositories {#modules}

The DWARPH project is split into several interconnected components.
The [DWARPHs GitHub organisation](`r GITHUB_ORG_URL`) hosts the material (source code, schedules, CAD files, analysis) for each of them.

## How the parts fit together {#architecture}

A DWARPH deployment has two halves: any number of **devices**, and one **operator workstation** running the Commander. There is no central server and no cloud component; everything happens on the local network. (A large set-up can add the optional online hub, Section \@ref(hub-module), but nothing on the local network depends on it.)

* Each **device** boots, joins the WiFi network named in its schedule, and starts executing that schedule autonomously. It keeps running whether or not anyone is watching — images and logs accumulate on its SD card.
* Each device **announces itself** over mDNS/ZeroConf, under a service name containing `dwarph`.
* Each device **publishes telemetry** to an MQTT broker once per second, and **serves a REST API** over HTTP.
* The **Commander** discovers devices by mDNS, subscribes to their MQTT topics for the live view, and uses REST for anything that needs a request/response exchange: fetching images, uploading a new schedule, starting and stopping the scheduler, streaming video, updating firmware.

The split matters in practice: MQTT carries the fast, lossy, broadcast-style state that a dashboard needs (temperature, setpoint, heater output), while REST carries the deliberate operations. A device with no broker configured still works fully over REST; MQTT is optional.

## The device firmware {#firmware}

`DWARPH-firmware` is an [ESP-IDF](https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esp-idf/en/stable/esp32/get-started/index.html) project targeting the ESP32-S3. Its main responsibilities:

* **Scheduler** (`main/scheduler`) --- parses `schedule.json`, and interpolates between setpoints to produce the temperature and light target for the current moment. This is the component that turns a static configuration file into a running experiment; it is documented in Chapter \@ref(manual).
* **Heater controller and PID** (`main/heater_controller.h`, `main/PID`) --- regulates the heating ring against the scheduled temperature. Setpoints are clamped to 10--50 °C in firmware as a safety measure.
* **Light controller** (`main/light_contoroller.hpp`, `main/led_board`) --- drives the red, blue and white channels, each on a 0.0--1.0 scale.
* **Camera** (`main/camera.h`, `main/camera_pins.h`) --- time-lapse capture at the configured interval, with a selectable focus mode. Uses a modified OV5640 autofocus driver alongside the Espressif camera component.
* **REST API** (`main/api`) --- see Section \@ref(rest-api).
* **Storage and logging** (`main/sd_card.h`, `main/logger_task`) --- images and logs are written to an SD card, under a per-device folder named after the device ID.
* **Supporting services** --- WiFi (`main/wifi_handler.h`), RTC and NTP time synchronisation (`main/RTC`, `main/time_functions.h`), an OLED status display (`main/96OLED4PINIIC.h`), and boot diagnostics.

## The Commander {#gui}

`DWARPH-commander` is a Python/Tkinter application that turns a network of devices into a single dashboard.

* `discovery.py` --- ZeroConf discovery and device record tracking
* `mqtt_service.py` --- MQTT connection, subscription and queueing
* `http_client.py` --- REST request helpers
* `dashboard_controller.py` --- orchestrates discovery and MQTT processing
* `state_store.py` --- central device/detail state store the UI binds to
* `device_card.py` --- the per-device card widget
* `device_detail_window.py` --- per-device detail, actions and API console
* `app.py` --- application shell and window composition

What it gives an operator is covered in Chapter \@ref(manual).

## Image analysis: DWARPH-CV {#ml-module}

The purpose of the imaging is quantitative: turning a time-lapse of a growth chamber into per-frame measurements of the duckweed population, and relating those to the conditions the device recorded alongside them.
`DWARPH-CV` is a Python package (`dwarph_cv`) with a single command, `dwarph-cv`, that does this on the folders the Commander mirrors from the devices:

* **Segmentation** (`dwarph-cv segment`) --- a U-Net with a ResNet34 encoder outputs a duckweed mask for every image, and the coverage (fraction of the image that is duckweed) in a table. It runs on whole 1920×1920 images, on a GPU or a CPU.
* **Ring reference** (`dwarph-cv ring`, `dwarph-cv ring-coverage`) --- finds the red reference ring in each image and solves the camera pose, giving the camera's distance and tilt for each frame. The ring also bounds the growing area: coverage is reported as the proportion of the area inside the ring that duckweed covers, which does not depend on the camera's distance.
* **Training** (`dwarph-cv train`, optional) --- leave-one-device-out training and evaluation, and training on all data for a release.
* **Annotation** (`dwarph-cv annotate`, optional) --- an interactive SAM 2.1 tool to make ground-truth masks for whole time-lapse series: click on one frame, propagate through the following frames, correct where needed.

```{r segmentation-timelapse, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="The platform, then one week of device `C4E408` with the released segmentation model: the image (left), the model's mask with the inner edge of the reference ring in red (right), and the proportion of the ring covered by duckweed over time (below), one frame per hour. The image shows the program's set temperature and light levels; grey bands in the graph are the program's nights (all lights off), which follow the experiment's schedule rather than the clock. Made with `scripts/make_timelapse.py`."}
knitr::include_graphics("assets/duckweed_segmentation_C4E408.webp")
```

The data and the model are published on Zenodo:

* the **DWARPH duckweed segmentation dataset** v1.0: 13,581 images from 7 devices with their ground-truth masks and metadata, [doi:10.5281/zenodo.24164026](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24164026);
* the **DWARPH segmentation weights** (`unet_r34_duckweed` v1.0), trained on all of that dataset, [doi:10.5281/zenodo.24164133](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24164133). Tested on a device it has not seen (leave-one-device-out), the same training reaches an IoU of 0.976 ± 0.007. `dwarph-cv segment` downloads the model on first use and checks its checksum; you can also give it your own weights file.

Installation is described in Section \@ref(build-cv).

## The online hub (optional): DWARPH-hub {#hub-module}

**You do not need the hub to run DWARPH.** A device, the Commander and DWARPH-CV on one computer
make a complete set-up. The hub is for **large scale**: many devices, several labs or rooms,
experiments that several people follow, or image analysis that should keep up by itself.

`DWARPH-hub` is a server (one Linux machine, plus an S3-compatible bucket for the images) that:

* **collects** every device's images and their sidecar files from the labs' mirrors, checking each
  one against the checksum its device recorded. The bucket is the source of truth for images,
  so the hub's database can be rebuilt from it;
* **gets them analysed**: DWARPH-CV workers, on any computer with a GPU, take images from the
  hub's queue, run the ring detection and the segmentation in one pass, and send back the results
  and the masks. When a new model or ring version is released, every image is analysed again
  with it, and the old results are kept;
* **organises experiments as projects**: a table with one row per experiment (a device, a start
  and an end) and your own typed columns (genotype, treatment, ...), with every change kept as a
  revision. People are enrolled in a project as viewer, manager or owner;
* **shows them**: devices or experiments over time, by date or by days since each experiment
  started, with the images and their masks one click away (Section \@ref(hub)).

It uses the same building blocks as the EntoScan cabinet: FastAPI, Postgres, S3 object storage,
Authentik for signing in, and Caddy for HTTPS, as docker compose stacks. The repository also
holds the **local store** (`local/`, formerly DWARPH_DB): a catalogue and timeline viewer for one
computer, without a server.

Deploying it, and connecting Commanders and workers to it, is described in Section
\@ref(build-hub).

## Manuscript {#manuscript-module}

*Planned --- this repository does not exist yet.*

`DWARPH-manuscript` is intended to hold the material and experiments for the method publication describing the platform, following the same pattern as the rest of the project: the analysis that produces the figures lives in the open, next to the code it describes.
